payload.source_label: If contaminant mass is not conserved, the conservation law must contain source terms

contract.statement: This contract is audited only under the coordinator-selected interpretation under the broad user objective; it is not a literal detailed user reply or a printed-source hypothesis. Original source account: For a contaminant carried through a one-dimensional pipe by fluid with constant velocity ū, q(x,t) is its scalar concentration or density [printed page 1, example preceding (1.2)]. When contaminant mass is conserved, its flux is f(q) = ūq and its governing scalar advection equation is q_t + ūq_x = 0 [printed page 4, contaminant example after (1.10), referring to (1.2)]. Conservation balances the rate of change of the quantity inside an interval with flux at its first endpoint minus flux at its second endpoint; it does not require the quantity in that interval to remain constant [printed page 4, (1.10) and its interpretation]. If contaminant mass is not conserved, for example because of chemical reactions, the law must also include source terms, whose form is not specified in this passage [printed page 4, sentence following f(q) = ūq]. The surrounding discussion requires sufficient smoothness to derive the classical differential law from the integral law [printed page 4, Section 1.1.2]. Coordinator-selected refinement Q6-FIXED-REPRESENTATIVE-ITERATED-BALANCE-20260908, SHA-256 8658feb83ed55f4c7a4a5c64a95c45313814c44b62573372ea716b5c791e97f3: its exact model clauses and preserved source ambiguities below are part of this qualified contract, not additional printed-source assertions or literal user replies.
assumptions: The contaminant is advected by fluid through a one-dimensional pipe at constant velocity ū [raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, example preceding (1.2)].
For the homogeneous contaminant conservation law, contaminant mass is conserved as it flows down the pipe [raw PDF page 26, printed page 4, contaminant example after (1.10)].
For the separate nonconservative case, the total mass of contaminant is not conserved, for example because of chemical reactions [raw PDF page 26, printed page 4, sentence following f(q) = ūq].

Passing from the integral conservation law to its classical differential form requires q and f(q) to be sufficiently smooth; no precise regularity class is specified here [raw PDF page 26, printed page 4, opening of Section 1.1.2].
The selected passage is an explanatory physical example within Section 1.1.1, rather than a separately quantified theorem [raw PDF page 26, printed page 4, paragraph following (1.10)].

Conservation of contaminant mass does not mean that the mass inside a fixed interval is constant: the source explicitly permits change through endpoint fluxes [raw PDF page 26, printed page 4, interpretation of (1.10)].

The source refers to Chapter 2 for the derivation of the advection equation and to Section 2.5 and Chapter 17 for source terms; these referenced treatments are not included in the supplied images [raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, following (1.2); raw PDF page 26, printed page 4, nonconservation sentence].

Selected model [field_and_flux]: Use fixed pointwise functions q and production from real space x real time to R^1 (represented as Fin 1 -> R), and a supplied constant real speed. The contaminant flux is speed times the supplied state, with no sign restriction on production or speed.

Selected model [representatives]: The supplied q and production are the actual pointwise representatives used in all hypotheses, boundary evaluations and integrals. They are not equivalence classes modulo two-dimensional space-time null sets. No exceptional-time slice is silently replaced before classification or theorem application.

Selected model [measure_and_endpoints]: Use ordinary one-dimensional Lebesgue volume and its oriented interval integrals for every real finite spatial pair a,b and temporal pair s,t. Reversed endpoints are included with the usual oriented-integral sign; no finite global-space or global-time integral is required.
Selected model [mass_slice_condition]: For every real a,b,t, x -> q(x,t) is interval integrable on a..b. This is an every-time requirement on the fixed mass representative.

Selected model [boundary_flux_condition]: For every real x,s,t, tau -> speed * q(x,tau) is interval integrable on s..t. The actual value on each chosen spatial boundary is used; no quotient by space-time null sets identifies arbitrary boundary traces.
Selected model [production_slice_condition]: For every real a,b,t, x -> production(x,t) is interval integrable on a..b. This includes every exceptional time, not merely almost every time.

Selected model [iterated_production_condition]: For every real a,b,s,t, tau -> integral(a..b, production(x,tau) dx) is interval integrable on s..t. This is integrability of the signed spatial aggregate; it is not a hypothesis that the time integral of the spatial integral of the absolute production density is finite.

Selected model [domain_not_joint_L1]: These exact slice and signed-aggregate conditions define the selected analytic domain. Do not replace them by bare jointly space-time L1_loc, by an L1 equivalence class with chosen good slices, or by joint L1_loc plus unstated representative corrections. No equivalence between these different domains is asserted.

Selected model [balance_hypothesis]: For every real a,b,s,t, interval mass at t minus interval mass at s equals the time integral from s to t of speed*q(a,tau)-speed*q(b,tau), plus the time integral from s to t of the spatial production integral over a..b. The theorem assumes this actual sourced rectangle balance for the supplied fields.

Selected model [nonconservation_meaning]: Within that selected sourced model, failure of homogeneous rectangle conservation means that some finite oriented rectangle has nonzero integrated production. A nonzero raw production value at an isolated point is not the nonconservation criterion, and a changing mass in one interval is adjusted for its actual boundary exchange.

Selected model [mass_rate_scope]: For each fixed real a,b, the interval-mass function has derivative speed*q(a,t)-speed*q(b,t)+integral(a..b,production(x,t) dx) for almost every real t. The exceptional null set may depend on a,b. No derivative identity at every time, one common exceptional set for all intervals, or spatial differentiability of q is imposed.

Selected model [logical_scope]: The exact mass-defect identity and the two homogeneous/nonhomogeneous biconditionals are consequences inside the supplied sourced rectangle model. This does not assert existence of an admissible production density for every arbitrary nonconserving field, a chemical rate law, or pointwise uniqueness of production.
Selected model [exclusions]: General singular production measures remain outside Q6. No positivity, spatial classical derivative, joint regularity, or global integrability condition is added.

Preserved source ambiguity: The printed contaminant paragraph requires source terms when mass changes beyond transport, but does not specify a production function space, a sourced rectangle equation, representative treatment, or a nonzero criterion at this level of precision.

Preserved source ambiguity: The original Q6 phrase locally integrable production densities did not distinguish joint space-time local integrability from exact every-time slices and temporally integrable signed spatial aggregates.

Preserved source ambiguity: The reported exceptional-time-slice example remains an effective-domain distinction; it is not a counterexample to the conditional theorem and not evidence of genuine theorem strengthening.

Preserved source ambiguity: The almost-everywhere temporal convention and rectangle biconditionals remain interpretation-qualified and are not attributed as literal additional printed hypotheses or conclusions.
quantifiers: x is the spatial coordinate along the one-dimensional pipe and t is time; q(x,t) is the scalar contaminant concentration or density [raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, example preceding (1.2)].
ū is the constant fluid velocity in the contaminant example [raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, example preceding (1.2)].
x₁ and x₂ are arbitrary spatial endpoints in the integral conservation law [raw PDF page 26, printed page 4, 'for any two points' preceding (1.10)].
f is the flux function of the conserved state, specialized to f(q) = ūq for the contaminant [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, after (1.8); raw PDF page 26, printed page 4, contaminant example].
